---
title: "Standard Normal"
description: "The exact reference case and Monte Carlo calibration"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/populations.R")
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
population <- get_population("normal")
diagnostics <- read.csv("../results/diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- diagnostics[diagnostics$population == "normal", ]
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
selected_n <- c(1, 10, 100)
simulation <- simulate_population(population, selected_n, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
```

## 1. Question and prediction

How quickly does Normal happen when the parent population is already Standard Normal? It happens immediately. A linear combination of independent Normal variables is Normal, so the sample mean is exactly Normal at every positive sample size. The smallest defensible answer is therefore $n=1$.

## 2. Parent population

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-parent
#| fig-cap: "The Standard Normal parent is symmetric and light-tailed. It supplies the exact-shape reference used to distinguish simulation noise from meaningful departures elsewhere."
#| fig-alt: "A symmetric bell-shaped Standard Normal density centered at zero."
plot_parent_population(population)
```

## 3. Theory before simulation

For independent $X_i \sim N(0,1)$,

$$
\bar X_n \sim N\left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right).
$$

The center is 0 and the standard error is $1/\sqrt{n}$. No approximation is involved.

## 4. Simulation design

At every evaluated $n$, I generated 10,000 independent sample means with seed 631. The simulated diagnostics calibrate the amount of random fluctuation expected even when Normality is exact.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normal-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Normal diagnostics at three scales. Empirical center and SE remain close to exact theory; shape metrics fluctuate slightly because only 10,000 means are simulated."
normal_table <- page_results[page_results$n %in% selected_n, c("n", "simulated_mean", "simulated_se", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(normal_table) <- c("n", "Mean", "Empirical SE", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(normal_table, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

At $n=1$, the simulated mean is `r sprintf("%.4f", page_results$simulated_mean[page_results$n == 1])` and the empirical SE is `r sprintf("%.4f", page_results$simulated_se[page_results$n == 1])`. These are simulation errors around 0 and 1, not evidence against the exact theorem.

## 6. Shape across sample sizes

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-sampling
#| fig-cap: "Sampling distributions at n = 1, 10, and 100 with exact theoretical Normal overlays in dark gray. The scale contracts with n, but the bell shape is exact throughout, so n = 1 is already sufficient."
#| fig-alt: "Three symmetric bell-shaped histograms that narrow around zero as sample size increases."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Q-Q evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-qq
#| fig-cap: "Standardized Normal quantiles at three sample sizes closely follow the reference line. Small tail deviations show Monte Carlo noise, not a changing distributional shape."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels with points close to a straight diagonal line."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 8. Calibration bands

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normal-bands
#| tbl-cap: "Guidance bands calibrated from the largest Normal fluctuation, subject to practical floors. These bands guide later judgments but do not form a weighted score."
band_table <- bands
band_table$threshold <- round(band_table$threshold, 4)
knitr::kable(band_table, col.names = c("Metric", "Guidance threshold"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Normal shape diagnostics fluctuate around their targets rather than following a convergence trend. The red guidance lines quantify ordinary Monte Carlo noise under an exactly Normal law."
#| fig-alt: "Three diagnostic trajectories fluctuating at low levels across sample size."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(page_results, population, bands)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-se
#| fig-cap: "Empirical and exact theoretical standard errors agree across the grid. Both contract as one over the square root of n, independently of the already exact shape."
#| fig-alt: "Two nearly overlapping standard-error curves declining with sample size."
plot_se_comparison(page_results, population)
```

## 9. Decision and diagnostic agreement

**Decision: $n=1$.** Theory is decisive, and the numerical and graphical evidence agree. The calibration results show why a finite simulation should never be expected to produce exactly zero skewness, exactly zero excess kurtosis, or a perfect Q-Q line.

## 10. Limitation and surprise

The apparent roughness of a histogram depends on binning, and the largest simulated calibration fluctuation depends on the chosen grid. The important surprise is conceptual: increasing $n$ improves precision here, but it does not make the standardized shape more Normal. It was already Normal.
